title: AI bots ‘killed my business, cost me $50k’
full_text:
Meta’s use of AI chatbots for customer service is being branded a “hamster wheel of death” by embattled Australian small business owners, who face losing their livelihoods as a result of the tech giant’s lack of human support.
Business owners have told The Australian horror stories of Meta’s unresponsiveness after hackers took control of their accounts, leading to the closure of one business and costing an owner up to $50,000.
Remarkably, the social networking giant responded to questions by attempting to have journalists help fix the tech troubles for one of the frustrated business owners.
The outcry lends support to a bid from the Telecommunications Industry Ombudsman to expand its powers to deal with unresolved digital service problems, which are costing Australians at least $497m a year.
Art educator Ali Mutch and travel agent Simone Lewis rely on Meta’s platforms – Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp – as essential everyday tools to communicate with customers.
Ms Mutch, a TV presenter, started her art education business The Art Hive in January, quickly building up a solid customer base by engaging with people through Facebook and Instagram.
But in June, the Bunbury woman was locked out of Meta’s platforms and watched in horror as hackers used a credit card linked to her Meta account to spend more than $1700 to buy Facebook ads promoting compression socks in Vietnam.
After two weeks of wrangling with Meta’s AI “customer service” chatbots, she was able to reclaim her Facebook account, but she remained too scared to use it for months because the hackers’ profiles were still linked to it.
After 12 weeks of dealing with chatbots, she paid $280 for Meta Verified, allowing her to finally speak with a human customer service agent – but at the time of publication, the hackers’ remaining link to her page had not been fixed. Meta also deleted all of her Instagram accounts in a bungled effort to target the hackers.
“Every time I thought that I was speaking to someone, it was just an AI bot. I called it ‘the Meta hamster wheel of death’,” Ms Mutch said. “It was absolutely crippling and frustrating, and I almost went mad. I’d worked really hard ... to put a lot of Facebook advertising into reaching the community and into building my Instagram, and that just disappeared in a heartbeat.” Ms Mutch said she closed her photography business, Phoenix and Wren, because it had not been possible to reach anyone without her Meta accounts. Meta refunded money stolen by hackers, but Ms Mutch estimated the ordeal had cost her up to $50,000 after she was forced to cancel 10 holiday art workshops because she was unable to advertise.
Ms Lewis, who lives in Melbourne and runs travel agency On The Road Travel Group, relies on social media to stay in touch with clients jetting off overseas. After reporting a suspicious login to Meta, she was suddenly frozen out of her personal and business Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp accounts, triggering a gruelling weeks-long battle just to prove she was the real Simone Lewis.
Ms Lewis regained access to Facebook and Instagram, but had still been unable to regain access to her original WhatsApp at the time of publication.
“What I find crazy is that there appears to be no way to speak to an actual person at WhatsApp about the situation. Everything is automated, so when the automated review rejects your appeal, there seems to be nowhere else to go,” she said. “The lack of accessible human customer service is incredibly frustrating.” A June 2026 TIO report found unresolved digital service problems were costing the Australian community an estimated $497m a year. But Ombudsman Cynthia Gerber said the figure was “a pretty conservative estimate”.
When sked to respond to the experiences of Ms Mutch and Ms Lewis, Meta attempted to enlist these journalists in a last-ditch attempt to fix the issues. A Meta spokeswoman said: “We understand how frustrating it is when people can’t access their accounts ... We offer multiple pathways to resolve account issues across our platforms and encourage people to enable two-factor authentication or passkeys to protect their accounts ...”
